newsitem.title: UK: UK's Clarke pledges tax cuts,rates unchanged.
newsitem.headline: UK's Clarke pledges tax cuts,rates unchanged.

text.p: Britain left official interest rates unchanged Thursday and the finance minister repeated a pledge to bring the country's basic rate of tax down to 20 percent as soon as public finances allowed.

The Bank of England operated at unchanged dealing rates in the domestic money market, confirming finance minister Kenneth Clarke had decided to leave official base rates unchanged at 5-3/4 percent at Wednesday's monthly monetary meeting.

At a news conference spearheading the ruling Conservative Party's fall campaign for next year's general election, Clarke fiercly defended his decision to raise taxes in the first few budgets he presided over as Chancellor of the Exchequer.
"Yes, we took tough measures which involved some increases in taxation. We will continue on that tax cutting agenda when it is sensible to do so," he said.

Clarke said reducing the basic rate of income tax to 20 pence per pound for all people paying 24 pence now would cost the country around 7.0 billion pounds ($10.98 billion). He dismissed a pledge from the opposition Labour Party to cut the starting rate of tax to 10 or 15 percent as "incredible."

The Conservatives have been in power for 17 years, but for many months opinion polls have shown them trailing the Labour Party by more than 20 percentage points. The next general election must take place by May 1997 at the latest.

Many economists believe that another rate cut is still imminent, but said that for the moment the Bank's caution against igniting inflation pressures had overcome any temptation Clarke may have had to loosen monetary policy.

The Confederation of British Industry said in a survey released Thursday that annual retail sales rose once again in August, with the balance of firms reporting a rise in sales, the largest since November 1988.
